candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Epistle of Enoch (1 Enoch 91-108)
candidates.source_attribution: 1 Enoch 104:2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. Dan 12:3 + Mt 13:43.
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Epistle of Enoch (1 Enoch 91-108) (c. 100 BC)

'Be hopeful; for aforetime ye were put to shame through ill and affliction; but now ye shall shine as the lights of heaven, ye shall shine and ye shall be seen, and the portals of heaven shall be opened to you' — the Epistle's closing exhortation to the persecuted righteous. The 'shine as the lights of heaven' echoes Daniel 12:3 ('they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament') and anticipates Matthew 13:43 ('Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father'). Tewahedo eschatology preserves this glorification-by-shining as the proper image of the resurrection body: not pale ghost, not generic light, but glorified material radiance that is recognizably the individual person now made luminous.

1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Epistle of Enoch (1 Enoch 91-108) (c. 100 BC)

'Be hopeful, and cast not away your hope, for ye shall have great joy as the angels of heaven. What shall ye be obliged to do? Ye shall not have to hide on the day of the great judgement, and ye shall not be found as sinners' — hope-oracle promising the righteous won't have to hide at judgment. The 'no-hiding-at-judgment' assurance is preserved in Tewahedo mystical theology as the eschatological correlate of the righteous having nothing-to-fear-in-the-light: those whose deeds are done in light fear no light.

candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Epistle of Enoch (1 Enoch 91-108) (c. 100 BC)

'And now I know this mystery, that sinners will alter and pervert the words of righteousness in many ways, and will speak wicked words, and lie, and practise great deceits, and write books concerning their words' — the textual-corruption warning. Tewahedo manuscript culture treats this verse with extraordinary seriousness: the entire monastic-scribal preservation enterprise is partly defined by the conviction that texts CAN be corrupted ('sinners will alter') and must be guarded. The Tewahedo Mäṣḥafä Hēnok preservation through 16 centuries when every other communion lost it is the practical witness to this verse.

candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Epistle of Enoch (1 Enoch 91-108) (c. 100 BC)

'And now I know this mystery, that to the righteous and wise shall the books be given as a joy and as a recompense and as a wisdom, and they shall believe in them and rejoice in them; and then shall all the righteous who have learnt therefrom all the paths of uprightness be recompensed' — books given to the righteous as joy. The PERMANENT-GIFT-OF-BOOKS theme is central to Tewahedo spirituality: monastic manuscript copying is not a chore but a JOY-FORM. The Tewahedo Mäṣḥafä Sǝbḥata Foṣǝlt prayer treats text-preservation as participation in the heavenly liturgy.
